analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacists, wholesalers, and individuals legally import cheaper prescription drugs from other developed countries.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill never got a hearing or a vote — it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in January 2005 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal rules so that Americans could buy prescription drugs from Canada, the European Union, and other countries where the same medicines sell for far less. It required exporters to register with the FDA, submit to inspections, use counterfeit-resistant packaging, and barred drug makers from punishing sellers who import. It never moved beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, especially seniors and people on long-term prescriptions, who pay the highest drug prices in the world. The bill's own findings say Americans pay up to 1000% more for some prescriptions than consumers abroad, and claim open markets could save consumers at least $635 billion a year. Pharmacies, wholesalers, and licensed internet pharmacies that wanted to sell lower-cost imported drugs would also gain a legal market.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write rules within 180 days permitting pharmacists, pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals to import qualifying drugs from countries with equivalent drug-safety systems [S2].

Lets individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply of a qualifying drug with a valid prescription, and creates a public list of registered exporters plus a toll-free number and website so people can verify a seller is legitimate [S3].

Makes it unlawful for a manufacturer to discriminate against importers — by charging them higher prices, cutting off their supply, or changing the drug's formulation to block importation — with enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general, including triple damages [S3].
Declares that selling or importing a patented drug first sold abroad under the patent owner's authority is not patent infringement, removing a legal tool used to block imports [S2].
Requires counterfeit-resistant packaging on all prescription drugs, similar to anti-counterfeit features on U.S. currency, taking effect 180 days after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose ability to charge Americans far more than foreign buyers would be undercut by a legal parallel import market. They would also bear registration compliance and packaging-security costs, and could face FTC and state enforcement actions for discriminatory conduct.

drawbacks.text: Safety risk: imported drugs travel outside the normal U.S. supply chain, and critics have long argued some would be counterfeit, substandard, or mislabeled even with inspections. The bill itself limits the risk by excluding narcotics, biologics, refrigerated drugs, and photoreactive drugs, and by requiring counterfeit-resistant packaging — but a well-designed system still depends on inspections actually catching problems [S3].

Drug makers could respond by restricting sales to exporting countries, since the bill cannot force a manufacturer to sell a drug in any country at all, which could limit how much supply is actually available to import [S3].

The program needs sustained FDA funding and staffing: registration fees are capped at 1% of the total price of drugs exported to the U.S., and the Secretary sets fees each year based on enforcement costs, so underfunding could leave inspections thin [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings for consumers are very large and the bill addressed the chief objection — counterfeits and unsafe imports — with exporter registration, FDA inspections, packaging-security rules, and a public registry of approved sellers. The main honest concern is execution: the system would only be as safe as its inspections, and manufacturers could shrink the supply available abroad. Still, this is a serious, safety-conscious attempt to let Americans pay what other developed countries pay for the same pills.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in early 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the Pharmaceutical Market Access Act of 2005 on January 24, 2005, with three original cosponsors: Sen. Ken Salazar, Sen. John Thune, and Sen. Jim DeMint [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S1].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill was bipartisan: its four cosponsors split 2 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept their legal ability to charge Americans much higher prices than consumers in other countries pay, and retained the ability to restrict supplies to any seller who imported cheaper drugs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept high U.S. prices

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its four cosponsors split evenly between two Democrats and two Republicans, and it died in committee rather than on party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have opened a legal import channel for the same FDA-approved drugs sold far cheaper abroad, and explicitly barred manufacturers from punishing importers with higher prices, supply cutoffs, or reformulated products. Americans pay the world's highest drug prices in part because this parallel-import channel is closed.

industries.industry: Pharmacies, wholesalers, and licensed internet pharmacies
industries.note: They would gain a legal business importing and selling lower-cost qualifying drugs, with an FDA registry of legitimate exporters to reassure customers. Their gain comes directly from lower prices for the people buying the drugs.
The bill requires counterfeit-resistant, currency-style security features on all prescription drug packaging, creating a compliance market for anti-counterfeit packaging technology.
